raw_case_text: A five-year-old boy, a case of standard-risk ALL with t(12,21), developed a prolonged course of intermittent fever and productive cough at the end of the second year of maintenance chemotherapy. He was receiving chemotherapy protocol as ALL-BFM-90 with some modifications. Induction therapy consisted of vincristine, prednisone, doxorubicin, L-asparaginase (L-ASP) [(10,000 IU/m2), twice a week], and intrathecal chemotherapy, followed by consolidation therapy including cytarabine, L-Asp, etoposide, and intermediate dose methotrexate (1 g/m2) with leucovorin. Reinduction therapy was similar to induction therapy except that daunorubicin was substituted for doxorubicin and dexamethasone for prednisone, respectively. Cranial radiotherapy was not given to the patient. Continuation therapy consisted of 6-mercaptopurine and methotrexate along with vincristine and prednisone every three weeks. A thorough investigation was conducted for evaluation of the fever and cough. A bone marrow examination was compatible with remission; a chest computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated diffuse patchy alveolar infiltrations. Investigation for fungal infections, including imaging studies and serum galactomannan assay, was negative, whereas cytomegalovirus pp65 assay on the sputum was indicated to be positive. Hence, he was determined to receive a course of ganciclovir along with the broad spectrum antibiotics including ceftazidime and vancomycin. The fever and cough improved significantly, and he was discharged after three weeks of treatment. Two days later, he came back with a severe dysuria and macroscopic haematuria. Aggressive hydration to ensure a urine output of 4-5 litres/day with 1/3 normal saline was started for the patient. His platelet counts and coagulation profile were normal. An imaging study of the urinary system, including a contrast enhanced abdominopelvic CT scan, showed a very thick walled bladder with distinct layering, perivesicular stranding, and intravesical clots [Figure 1(A)]. There was no recent history of treatment with cyclophosphamide in the patient. Accordingly, a urine sample was checked for BKV by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which was positive with increased loads to 1 x 105 copies/ml. At the same time, urine was also checked by PCR for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and adenovirus, which were negative. In addition, complementary for diagnosis, urine was examined for observation of decoy cells that were positive on centrifuged spot urine sample of the patient (Figure 2). The patient's plasma was also tested and showed positive viraemia with BKV with 3,000 copies/ml of plasma. The patient was so frustrated that urinary catheterisation was inserted for the child through which bladder irrigation was performed. He also received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), intravenous ciprofloxacin, and a combination of urinary antispasmodics; oxybutynin and phenazopyridine as local urinary analgesic to help in providing immediate symptomatic relief. The symptoms started to subside slowly so that during 10-12 weeks of conventional therapy, a decrease in bladder wall thickness was observed on repeated CT scans [Figure 1(B) and (C)]. Likewise, urine BK viral load started to decline; however, as mild degrees of dysuria was persistent for almost two months, the child discharged with oral ciprofloxacin and topical application of lidocaine and a mild steroid cream for symptomatic relief.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy with standard-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented at the end of his second year of maintenance chemotherapy with prolonged intermittent fever and productive cough, followed 2 days after hospital discharge by severe dysuria and macroscopic hematuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Receiving maintenance chemotherapy (6-mercaptopurine and methotrexate with q3w vincristine and prednisone under a modified ALL-BFM-90 protocol without cranial irradiation or recent cyclophosphamide) for t(12;21)-positive standard-risk ALL, the patient developed prolonged intermittent fever and productive cough at the end of year 2 of maintenance. Following a 3-week hospitalization and treatment for CMV respiratory infection with ganciclovir, ceftazidime, and vancomycin, he was discharged improved, only to return 2 days later with severe dysuria and frank macroscopic hematuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: Standard-risk t(12;21)-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in complete bone marrow remission at the end of year 2 of modified ALL-BFM-90 maintenance chemotherapy (prior induction with vincristine, prednisone, doxorubicin, L-asparaginase, and intrathecal therapy; consolidation with cytarabine, L-asparaginase, etoposide, and intermediate-dose methotrexate; reinduction with daunorubicin and dexamethasone; no recent cyclophosphamide exposure).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial episode: prolonged intermittent fever and productive cough. Readmission (2 days post-discharge): severe dysuria and macroscopic hematuria.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: febrile with productive cough. Readmission: severe dysuria and gross hematuria requiring urinary catheterization and continuous bladder irrigation.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: serum galactomannan assay negative; sputum cytomegalovirus (CMV) pp65 antigenemia assay positive. Readmission: normal platelet count and coagulation profile; centrifuged spot urine microscopy positive for viral 'decoy cells' (persistent mild dysuria for ~2 months).
objective.advanced_workup: Initial admission: bone marrow aspirate confirmed complete leukemia remission; chest CT demonstrated diffuse patchy alveolar infiltrations. Readmission: contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT showed severe bladder wall thickening with distinct mucosal layering, perivesical fat stranding, and intravesical blood clots (which progressively resolved over 10-12 weeks on repeat CT scans). Quantitative real-time PCR on readmission was positive for BK polyomavirus (BKV) in urine (1 x 10^5 copies/mL) and plasma (3,000 copies/mL), while urine PCRs for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and adenovirus were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed initially with cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis (confirmed by positive sputum CMV pp65 antigenemia and diffuse patchy alveolar infiltrates on chest CT with negative fungal galactomannan), which resolved after 3 weeks of intravenous ganciclovir, ceftazidime, and vancomycin; subsequently diagnosed on readmission with late-onset BK virus (BKV)-associated severe hemorrhagic cystitis (confirmed by urine decoy cells, urine BKV PCR load of 1 x 10^5 copies/mL, plasma BKV viremia of 3,000 copies/mL, and negative urine CMV and adenovirus PCRs). Hemorrhagic cystitis was managed with hyperhydration (4-5 L/day), urinary catheterization with bladder irrigation, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), intravenous/oral ciprofloxacin, oral oxybutynin and phenazopyridine, and topical lidocaine/mild steroid cream, achieving progressive resolution of bladder wall thickening on CT and declining urine BKV loads over 10-12 weeks.
